finding.claim: Unauthenticated blind SSRF: the /hooks/test route on the pub router sends a POST to an arbitrary attacker-supplied URL. The response returns only the status code, so the attacker gets a success/failure oracle.
finding.source: req.body.callback (routes.js:20), supplied by any HTTP caller. No authentication is applied in this file to the pub router.
finding.sink: axios.post(req.body.callback, { ping: true }) at routes.js:20. Outbound POST from the server to an arbitrary URL.

trace.note: pub.post('/hooks/test') route handler; no auth middleware on the pub router in this file
req.body.callback flows directly into axios.post as the URL; body is fixed to { ping: true }, method fixed to POST

res.json({ status: r.status }) returns the status code to the caller, giving a success/failure oracle. Non-2xx responses make axios throw, which is uncaught in Express 4, so the response hangs or errors

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or session check on the pub router within this file (mount code not in repo, so deployed auth is unverified). No scheme, host, IP-range, or port allowlist. No DNS or redirect controls; axios follows redirects by default. No try/catch around axios.post. Attacker controls URL only, not method or body. Installed axios version and its supported URL schemes were not verified (no package.json in repo).

verdict.guard_found: none. routes.js:19-21 has no validation, allowlist, or try/catch. The only guard in the file, requireAdmin (routes.js:7-10), is applied via admin.use at routes.js:12 and does not cover the pub router. The mount code is not in the repo, so auth applied at mount time cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: routes.js:20 passes req.body.callback straight to axios.post with no validation, and routes.js:19 sits on the pub router, which has no auth in this file (requireAdmin at routes.js:12 applies only to admin), so an unauthenticated caller controls the outbound URL and gets a status-code oracle at routes.js:21. The only open question is whether the deployed mount adds auth, which the repo cannot show; the claim's line references, method and body are all accurate.

finding.claim: Admin-gated SSRF: the /diagnostics/fetch route makes a GET request to an arbitrary URL supplied in the query string and returns the status code. Access requires an admin session, so the attacker must already hold admin privileges.
finding.source: req.query.url (routes.js:15), supplied by the caller. Only callers with session.role === 'admin' can reach the route.
finding.sink: axios.get(req.query.url) at routes.js:15. Outbound GET from the server to an arbitrary URL.

trace.note: admin.use(requireAdmin) applies the admin check to all admin routes
requireAdmin checks req.session.role === 'admin' and returns 403 otherwise
req.query.url is passed directly to axios.get with no validation
res.json({ status: r.status }) returns the status code to the caller, giving an oracle for internal hosts

finding.guards_checked: Authorization gate: requireAdmin at routes.js:7-12 (role check only, not an input check). No scheme, host, IP-range, or port allowlist. Redirects followed by default, so a URL allowlist on the initial request would not stop a redirect to an internal address. No try/catch around axios.get. Severity is lower than SSRF-1 because the caller must already be an admin; the admin model is defined outside this repo.

verdict.guard_found: No URL/host/scheme allowlist before the sink at routes.js:15. The admin gate is a role check (routes.js:7-12: requireAdmin at line 8 and admin.use at line 12), which is an authorization gate, not an input validation guard.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (routes.js:12 applies requireAdmin, line 8 returns 403 for non-admins, line 15 passes req.query.url straight to axios.get, line 16 returns the status), but the source is not controllable by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker: routes.js:8 restricts the route to session.role === 'admin', so the claimed attacker must already hold admin rights, which fails the source check and makes this a hardening issue rather than a vulnerability in the stated threat model.
